scene.speaker: nova
scene.bubble: Welcome to B2 First! This unit is about the past shaping the present — get ready for mixed conditionals, wish and if only, and your first Use of English tasks.
scene.intro: Welcome to B2 First. This year the Inspiring Nordic project asks harder questions about society and fairness — and about how much our past decides our present. In this unit our reading club discusses Dickens's Oliver Twist in the format of Reading Part 5, listens to Miss Vega in the format of Listening Part 2, learns mixed conditionals to connect a past cause with a present result, adds wish and if only for regrets, and writes your first Part 1 essay. If only... two words that carry a whole unit. Let's begin.

activities.title: Speaking — Parts 1 and 2. Talk with a partner, then record yourself.

tips.expect: Part 1 (2 minutes): the examiner asks you and your partner questions about yourselves — studies, family, plans. Part 2 (about 4 minutes for the pair): each of you talks alone for about a minute about two of three photographs, answering the question printed above them; then your partner answers a short question about your photographs in about 30 seconds.
how: In Part 1, give a reason or a short example with your answer — don't just say yes or no.
In Part 2, don't describe all three photographs: choose two, compare them and answer the question. Use link words like whereas, while or both.
Speculate even when you're not sure: she might be…, perhaps he's thinking about….
Keep talking for the full minute. If you finish saying everything about one photo, move straight to the other.
tips.remember: There is no 'correct' story behind the photographs. You are marked on your language, not on guessing what is really happening.

data.text: Part 1: talk about decisions, family and plans. Part 2: compare two photographs and say what decision each person might be facing.

parts.title: Interview
prompts: Tell me about a decision you made recently. Was it easy or difficult to make?
Is there something in your life you would do differently if you could go back? Why?
Do you think family has the biggest influence on who we become, or is it something else?
Who is someone whose past you find inspiring, and why?

parts.title: Long turn
parts.question: Compare the two photographs and say what decision each person might be facing or have faced and how their life might be different if they had chosen differently.

pictures.caption: a teenager looking at two paths through a forest
an elderly woman looking through an old photo album

parts.partner: Which of these situations do you think is hardest to think about — choosing a path now, or looking back at old choices? (about 30 seconds)

Comparing: While the teenager is…, the woman is…
In one picture…, but in the other…
Giving your view: If I were in that situation, I would…

activities.title: Reading and Use of English Part 5 — multiple choice. Read the essay and choose the answer that fits best.

tips.expect: One text of about 500–650 words followed by six four-option questions. They test main idea, detail, opinion, attitude and simple inference. The questions follow the order of the text.
how: Read the whole text once, fairly quickly, to get the general idea and the writer's attitude.
For each question, find the part of the text it refers to and read it closely. The correct option paraphrases the text; wrong options often reuse words from the text but change the meaning.
Don't choose an option just because it sounds true in general — check it against exactly what the text says.
tips.remember: The six questions follow the order of the text. If you get stuck, look near the place where the previous answer came from.

data.title: If only he had chosen differently
data.author: liam
data.text:
Our B2 reading club has just finished Oliver Twist, and the conversation afterwards was louder than usual. Everyone had an opinion about the same question: how much of what happens to us is really our own doing, and how much is simply the circumstances we are born into?

Nancy is the character we argued about the longest. She grows up among thieves, and by the time the story begins she has already made choices that trap her — she stays loyal to Bill Sikes even though he treats her cruelly, and she risks everything to protect Oliver. Nadia said that if Nancy had been given a different upbringing, she would probably be a completely different woman today; her life looks less like a decision and more like a consequence of everything that came before it. Mateo disagreed. In his view, Nancy still has choices in front of her, and the moment when she decides to warn Mr Brownlow about Oliver proves it. “If she truly believed she had no freedom left,” he argued, “she wouldn't have taken that risk.”

What struck most of us, though, was a smaller scene: years later, Mr Bumble admits that he regrets how he treated Oliver as a child. He never quite says he wishes he had acted differently, but Dickens lets us see the discomfort underneath his excuses. Sofía pointed out that this is what makes the novel feel modern rather than old-fashioned: it isn't only interested in the children who suffer injustice, but also in the adults who caused it and now have to live with what they did.

Talking about the book gave us a reason to try out a piece of grammar we had just learnt: the mixed conditional, which connects a past cause to a present result in a single sentence. “If Nancy had grown up somewhere kinder, she wouldn't be trapped now,” Nadia said, testing the structure out loud. Mateo tried the opposite direction: “If Bumble weren't so proud today, he would have apologised long ago.” Miss Vega laughed and said the grammar had clearly done its job: nobody in the room was describing the past and the present separately any more; they were describing how one produces the other.

Miss Vega then asked us to think about our own “Bumble moments” — decisions we might look back on differently one day. Nobody wanted to answer first. Eventually Liam admitted that he had once refused to help a classmate with a project because he assumed the boy would not bother trying. “If I hadn't judged him so quickly,” he said, “we might actually be friends now.” It was a small confession, but the room went quiet in the way it does when someone says something everyone secretly recognises.

This is, in the end, the real subject of Oliver Twist: not poverty or crime as isolated problems, but the long, invisible line that connects a difficult beginning to an uncertain future — and the shorter, more private line that connects an unkind decision to the person we later become. Dickens never lets Oliver's good nature feel automatic; it survives in spite of everything, which is exactly why the ending feels earned rather than convenient.

Society, the club agreed, still asks the same question it asked in 1837: do we owe more patience to people whose circumstances we haven't lived through? Nobody left with a tidy answer, and Miss Vega seemed pleased about that. A novel that gives you an easy answer, she told us, probably was not asking a difficult enough question in the first place.
data.script: Our B2 reading club has just finished Oliver Twist. Everyone had an opinion about how much of what happens to us is really our own doing, and how much is simply the circumstances we are born into. Nancy is the character we argued about the longest. Nadia said that if Nancy had been given a different upbringing, she would probably be a different woman today. Mateo disagreed, saying Nancy still has choices, and the moment she warns Mr Brownlow proves it. What struck most of us was Mr Bumble, who years later regrets how he treated Oliver as a child, even if he never quite says so. Sofía said this is what makes the novel feel modern: it cares about the adults who caused injustice, not only the children who suffered it. Talking about the book gave us a reason to try out mixed conditionals, connecting a past cause to a present result. Miss Vega then asked us to think about our own Bumble moments. Liam admitted that if he hadn't judged a classmate so quickly, they might be friends now. In the end, Oliver Twist connects a difficult beginning to an uncertain future, and an unkind decision to the person we later become. Society, the club agreed, still asks the same question it asked in 1837, and nobody left with a tidy answer.

options: The students had memorised the rule correctly.
The students were now describing how the past shapes the present, not two separate stories.

The students preferred grammar practice to discussing the novel.

options: To criticise the way Liam usually treats his classmates.
To prove that Liam has changed his opinion of the novel.

data.title: Mixed conditionals
data.can: I can use a mixed conditional to connect a past cause with a present result, or a present state with a past result.
data.intro: A mixed conditional combines two different time frames in one sentence — usually a past cause with a present result, sometimes the other way round. In the reading, Nadia and Mateo both used this structure to talk about Nancy and Bumble: If Nancy had grown up somewhere kinder, she wouldn't be trapped now.

examples.text: If Oliver had been born into a wealthier family, he wouldn't be struggling now.
If Nancy hadn't grown up among thieves, she wouldn't be trapped today.
If I were braver, I would have spoken up yesterday.
If he weren't so proud, he would have apologised long ago.
If we understood each other's stories better, the world would have been kinder to people like Oliver.

rules: Past cause → present result: If + past perfect, … would + base verb (now).
Present state → past result: If + past simple, … would have + past participle.
Use were instead of was for I / he / she / it in this structure: If she were braver…
Only mix the tenses when the two moments really are different — don't mix them just for variety.
This structure is a close relative of Language focus 2 in this unit: wish / if only also use the past perfect to look back at something that still matters now.

items.sentence: If she had studied harder, she ___ better grades now.
If I weren't so busy this week, I ___ to help you yesterday.
If they had saved more money, they ___ a house by now.
If he ___ so stubborn, he would have accepted our help months ago.
If we had understood the risk, we ___ more careful now.

activities.title: Reading and Use of English Part 4 — key word transformations

tips.expect: Six sentences. For each one you complete a second sentence so that it means the same as the first, using a given key word. You write between two and five words, including the key word, which you must not change. Here the six items focus on mixed conditionals and on wish / if only.
how: Decide first what is being tested: a past cause with a present result, a present state with a past result, or a regret with wish / if only.
Write the whole gap, then read the complete second sentence: does it mean exactly the same as the first? Is the key word unchanged?
Count your words. A contraction such as hadn't counts as one word.
tips.remember: The key word must appear only once, inside the gap — not repeated in the part of the sentence that is already given.

data.instructions: Complete the second sentence so that it has a similar meaning to the first sentence, using the word given. Do not change the word given. You must use between two and five words, including the word given.

items.first: Nancy is trapped now because of the way she grew up.
items.second_end: up differently, she wouldn't be trapped now.

items.first: Liam didn't get to know his classmate because he judged him too quickly.
items.second_end: his classmate so quickly, they might be friends today.

items.first: I'm sorry I didn't help my friend sooner.
We regret arguing so much last week.
I didn't apply for the scholarship because I'm not confident enough.
items.second_end: , I would have applied for the scholarship.

items.first: We have this problem today because they didn't plan properly.
items.second_end: , we wouldn't have this problem today.

activities.title: Listening Part 2 — sentence completion. Complete the sentences with a word or short phrase.

tips.expect: A monologue of about three minutes, introduced by a presenter. You complete eight sentences with a word or short phrase (no more than three words) that you hear. You hear the recording twice.
how: Before it starts, read the eight sentences and predict the kind of word that is missing: a noun? an adjective? a number?
The sentences follow the order of the recording. The words around the gap are often paraphrased, but the answer itself is the exact word you hear.
Write exactly what you hear, spelt correctly. Don't change the form of the word.
tips.remember: If you miss one gap, let it go and follow the next sentence. You get a second listening.

data.voice_note: Presenter + Miss Vega, teacher. Monologue with a short introduction.
data.script:
Presenter: Welcome back to B2 Voices. Today's talk comes from Miss Vega, who teaches English here at school, and it's called Small decisions, big consequences.
Miss Vega: Thank you. I want to start with something Charles Dickens understood very well: that a single moment, barely a page long, can decide the shape of an entire life. In Oliver Twist, that moment sometimes happens without the character even noticing it at the time.
Miss Vega: Take Mr Bumble. He treats a hungry child unkindly because, in his mind, that is simply how the workhouse operates. He doesn't see it as a decision. Years later, though, it clearly weighs on him, even if he never quite admits it out loud.
Miss Vega: I think the same thing happens outside novels. Most regrets don't come from huge, dramatic mistakes. They come from ordinary moments: a comment we didn't think twice about, an apology we kept putting off, an opportunity we let slide because we were tired or simply distracted.
Miss Vega: What makes these moments dangerous is exactly how small they feel. If a decision felt enormous, we would think carefully before making it. But a five-second choice rarely gets that kind of attention, and yet five seconds can shape years.
Miss Vega: So how should we deal with this? First, notice the pattern. The moment you catch yourself thinking it's not a big deal, that is exactly the moment worth slowing down for. Second, practise saying sorry quickly. An apology delayed by a week is far harder to give than one offered on the same day.
Miss Vega: Third, and this is the point my students always find hardest, accept that some decisions cannot be undone, only understood. Wishing you had acted differently is not the same as pretending that you did. Understanding a mistake honestly is what actually changes how you act next time.
Miss Vega: Finally, remember that circumstances explain a decision; they don't erase it completely. Bumble's cruelty grew out of a harsh system, and that context genuinely matters. But context is not an excuse that removes his responsibility; it is a reason to be more patient with people whose full story we don't know.
Miss Vega: For your project this term, I would like you to write about one small decision, yours or a character's, and trace its consequences forward. You will be surprised how far a five-second choice can travel.

In Oliver Twist, a single … can decide the shape of a whole life.
Mr Bumble treats a hungry child unkindly because he doesn't see it as a …
Miss Vega says most regrets come from … moments, not dramatic mistakes.
She says a five-second choice can shape …
An apology delayed by a week is harder to give than one offered on the same …
She says some decisions cannot be undone, only …
Miss Vega says a five-second choice can …

activities.title: Language focus 2 — wish / if only + past perfect

data.title: Wish / if only for regrets about the past
data.can: I can use wish / if only + past perfect to talk about something I regret, and I can see how this connects to mixed conditionals.
data.intro: In the reading, Mr Bumble never quite says he wishes he had acted differently — but that is exactly the structure behind this focus. We use wish or if only + past perfect to talk about something in the past that we regret, often because — like a mixed conditional — it still affects the present.

examples.text: I wish I had helped my classmate sooner.
examples.note: wish + past perfect: regret about my own past action

examples.text: If only Bumble had treated Oliver more kindly.
examples.note: if only is stronger and more emotional than wish

examples.text: She wishes she hadn't judged him so quickly.
If only we hadn't argued so much last week.
I wish I were more confident. (not: I wish I had been more confident, this year, right now)
examples.note: compare: wish + past simple = regret about the present, not the past

rules: Wish / if only + past perfect (had + participle) = regret about something that happened, or didn't happen, in the past: I wish I had studied harder.
If only is stronger and more emotional than wish; both use the same past perfect.
The negative regret uses hadn't + participle: If only I hadn't said that.
Don't confuse this with wish + past simple, which is a regret about the present: I wish I were taller (not about the past).
This structure is a cousin of the mixed conditional: both look back with a past perfect. Wish / if only simply leaves out the result clause, because the regret itself is the point.

items.sentence: I wish I ___ more attention in class yesterday.
If only she ___ to her parents before making the decision.
He wishes he ___ so rude to his friend last week.
If only we ___ earlier — we missed the whole first half.
I wish I ___ that comment; it really hurt her.

activities.title: Reading and Use of English Part 2 — open cloze. Write ONE word in each gap.

tips.expect: A short text of about 150–200 words with eight gaps. You write one word in each gap — no options are given. The missing words are mostly grammar words: articles, prepositions, auxiliaries, pronouns, relative pronouns, linking words.
how: Read the whole text first: the words before and after the gap usually decide the answer.
Check both sides of the gap: does it need a preposition after a verb, a relative pronoun, part of a fixed phrase like if only?
Only one word fits each gap, and contractions are not allowed.
tips.remember: Check your spelling. A correct word spelt wrongly scores nothing.

data.text: Nobody in our reading club found it easy to defend Mr Bumble, but Sofía insisted that we try, if only for the sake of a fair discussion. {1} she pointed out is that Bumble grew up inside the same harsh system {2} treated Oliver so badly, working long hours for a workhouse that valued discipline far more than kindness. None of this makes his behaviour acceptable, and Sofía was careful to say so — the point was to explain his cruelty {3} excusing it completely. Nadia disagreed at first: plenty of people, she said, survive difficult circumstances and never become cruel at all, {4} she eventually admitted that circumstances and personal responsibility can both be true at the same time. If only he {5} chosen kindness even once, the class agreed, the whole story {6} have felt very different, both for Oliver and for Bumble himself. Miss Vega closed the discussion by reminding us {7} regret is only useful {8} it eventually changes what we do next.

activities.title: Writing Part 1 — essay. Plan, write 140–190 words and hand it in.

tips.expect: Part 1 is compulsory. You are given a question and two notes, plus space for your own idea. You write an essay answering the question, using all three notes, in a formal or neutral register. 140–190 words.
how: Use all three notes, including your own idea — an essay that ignores one of them loses content marks.
Plan four short paragraphs: introduction (the question, no opinion yet) · note 1 · note 2 and your own idea · conclusion with your opinion.
Don't copy the notes word for word — put them in your own words.
Link your ideas with a range of devices, not only Firstly / Secondly but also What is more…, Another point worth considering is…
tips.remember: The examiner marks content, communicative achievement, organisation and language. An essay that ignores a note, or gives no clear opinion, loses content marks however good the English.

data.task:
Your class has been discussing this question: “Can people really change, or does our past always decide who we are?” Now your teacher has asked you to write an essay giving your opinion, using all the notes below.

Notes

  • upbringing
  • the choices we make later
  • ………………… (your own idea)

Write an essay answering the question above. You should explain your opinion, giving reasons in support of your answer.

Write your answer in 140–190 words in an appropriate style.
plan: Introduction (1–2 sentences): restate the question in your own words. No opinion yet.
Paragraph 2 — upbringing: how much family and early years shape a person, with a brief example.
Paragraph 3 — the choices we make later, plus your own idea (for example, the people we meet or the effort we make): show these can also change the outcome.
Conclusion: give your opinion clearly and say why, ideally connecting the two paragraphs.
checklist: I have used all three notes, including my own idea.
I have given my opinion clearly, with a reason.
My essay has four clear paragraphs.
The register is formal or neutral: no contractions, no very informal words.
I have used at least one mixed conditional or wish / if only sentence from this unit.
data.model:
A model answer (153 words). Notice the four paragraphs and how all three notes are used.

It is often said that our past decides who we are, and there is some truth in this: nobody chooses the family they are born into.

Our upbringing certainly matters. Children who grow up surrounded by encouragement usually find it easier to trust themselves later in life, while children who face hardship, like Oliver in Oliver Twist, often have to work much harder to build the same confidence.

However, the choices we make later can be just as powerful. Two people from the same difficult background can end up leading completely different lives, depending on the decisions they take and the people they choose to spend time with. If we had no freedom at all, nobody would ever surprise us.

In my view, then, our past shapes us but does not control us completely. What we do next always matters, and that is precisely why it is worth taking our decisions seriously.

activities.title: Speaking — Parts 3 and 4. Collaborative task and discussion. Record your best answer.

tips.expect: Part 3 (about 3 minutes: 2 to discuss, 1 to decide): you and your partner discuss five ideas with the help of a diagram, then reach a decision together. Part 4 (about 4 minutes): the examiner asks you both wider questions on the same theme.
how: In Part 3 you are marked on interacting, not on agreeing: ask your partner's opinion, respond to it, build on it.
Don't try to discuss all five ideas in depth — two or three, developed properly, is better than five in a rush.
In the decide minute, negotiate: Shall we agree that…? I see your point, but…
In Part 4, develop your answers: opinion → reason → example.
tips.remember: Look at your partner, not at the examiner, during Part 3. The examiner is listening, not talking.

data.text: Part 3: discuss how much these things shape who we become and decide which is hardest to overcome. Part 4: discuss change, decisions and looking back on the past.

parts.title: Collaborative task
parts.intro: Here are five things that can change the direction of a person's life. Talk to each other about how much each one really shapes who we become.
parts.centre: How much does each of these shape who we become?
spokes: the family we are born into
a teacher who believes in us
one big decision we make ourselves

parts.title: Further discussion
prompts: Do you think people can really change, or do we stay the same underneath?
Should schools spend more time helping students make good decisions?
Is it fair to judge someone without knowing their story, as Nadia said about Oliver Twist?

What advice would you give your younger self?

That's true up to a point, although…

homework.prompt: Write a short opinion paragraph (8–10 sentences) about a decision — yours or a character's from Oliver Twist — that still affects the present. Use at least two mixed conditionals and two wish / if only sentences (for example: 'If only I had spoken up, things would be different now.'). Capital letters and full stops!
